rows: Personal flotation devices reduce drowning risk when people fall overboard.
Fishing-vessel rules can require suitable PFDs or safety harnesses where there is a risk of falling overboard.
Lifejackets should be appropriate for the user, clothing, activity and operating conditions.
Equipment should be worn correctly rather than merely carried.
Inflatable lifejackets require inspection and servicing in accordance with their design and instructions.
Lights, whistles and other accessories may be required or appropriate for the operation.
Vessels need suitable means to recover a person from the water.
Operators should plan for man-overboard prevention, alerting and recovery.
Carrying a lifejacket does not prove it is suitable, serviceable, correctly fitted or being worn.
Safety conclusions require vessel type, activity, person, buoyancy, servicing, weather and recovery evidence.
Cold-water shock can rapidly impair breathing, movement and survival after immersion.
Preventing people from falling overboard is a primary control.
Suitable PFDs and harnesses can reduce the consequences of a fall overboard.
Man-overboard recovery needs to be planned for the vessel and crew.
Emergency drills should include realistic man-overboard response.
Rapid recovery is important because cold-water effects worsen with time.
Recovery equipment should be accessible and usable for an unconscious casualty.
Crew should understand alarm, manoeuvring, communication, recovery and aftercare arrangements.
Water temperature or distance from shore alone does not determine individual survival time.
Outcome depends on clothing, PFD, sea state, injury, fitness, alerting, recovery equipment and response time.
The Environment Agency issues flood alerts, flood warnings and severe flood warnings in England.
A flood alert means flooding is possible and people should prepare.
A flood warning means flooding is expected and action should be taken.
A severe flood warning indicates danger to life and significant disruption.
People can sign up for free warnings by text, phone or email where the service is available.
Warnings may cover flooding from rivers, the sea or groundwater depending on the area.
Current warning information should be checked regularly during elevated risk.
Official instructions should be followed and emergency services should be contacted where life is at risk.
A warning area does not prove that every property inside it will flood.
Property impact depends on flood source, level, defences, elevation, access, timing and current local conditions.
People and businesses handling controlled waste have a legal duty of care.
Waste must be stored securely to prevent escape or harm.
Waste should be transferred only to an authorised person.
The waste description must be accurate enough for the next holder to manage it safely.
Transfers generally require appropriate records such as waste transfer notes.
Businesses should check relevant waste-carrier, broker or permit status.
Suspected illegal or unsafe waste activity should be reported to the appropriate authority.
Records should be retained and made available as required.
A waste-transfer note does not prove that the waste description, carrier or final destination is lawful.
Compliance requires the actual waste, classification, storage, carrier, documentation, destination and permit evidence.
